title: Vaccination Rates and Family Barriers Among Children with Inflammatory Bowel Disease.
ehr_evidence: Indiana utilizes an online registry, the Children and Hoosier Immunization Program (CHIRP), which was used by research assistants to access vaccination records for each participant.
summary: Cross-sectional study comparing parental vaccine attitudes and vaccination rates between 50 children with IBD and 58 non-IBD children followed at a tertiary children's hospital in Indianapolis, Indiana.
key_findings: IBD families were more concerned than non-IBD families that vaccines could worsen their child's GI illness (36% vs 10%, P < 0.001)
IBD families were more concerned about vaccine effectiveness than non-IBD families (34% vs 12%, P = 0.001)
Concern about vaccine safety was higher in IBD but not statistically significant (40% vs 16%, P = 0.084)
89% of IBD children on biologic agents were missing the PPSV23 vaccine
51% of IBD and 50% of non-IBD children were missing at least one HPV-9 vaccine (P = 0.921)
56% of IBD and 67% of non-IBD children were missing an influenza vaccine from the 2018-2019 season (P = 0.264)
0% of IBD vs 11% of non-IBD children were missing the HBV series (P = 0.022)
captured_features: Vaccination registry records for HPV-9, influenza, PCV7/PCV13, PPSV23, MCV4, MMR, varicella, HBV, hepatitis A, and Tdap
Parent/caregiver Likert-scale survey responses on vaccine attitudes and concerns
Child and parent demographics (age, sex, race, ethnicity, caregiver education, household income)
IBD subtype (Crohn disease, ulcerative colitis, indeterminate colitis)
Current IBD medications (anti-TNF/infliximab, immunomodulator, steroids, mesalamine)
pathologies_diseases: Inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn disease, ulcerative colitis, indeterminate colitis)
Non-IBD GI conditions (abdominal pain, acid reflux, constipation)
population: 108 children ages 10-25 years (mean age 15 for IBD, 14 for non-IBD) and their caregivers, with (n=50) and without (n=58) IBD, followed at a tertiary children's hospital in Indianapolis, Indiana
exposure_domain: Vaccination uptake and parental vaccine attitudes/barriers
limitations: Single tertiary care center with relatively homogenous attitudes and physician practice
Small sample size with convenience sampling (most IBD patients were on infliximab)
Comparator group was non-IBD GI clinic patients rather than healthy controls
Highly selected sample (88% white, 52% of IBD parents with graduate education)
CHIRP registry mandated only since 2015, so early childhood vaccinations may be incomplete
data_availability_statement: Data stored and supported on figshare.com at https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.12442757.v1.
